render.title: The two mitochondrial membranes: permeability and purpose
render.body:
A mitochondrion is wrapped in two distinct membrane layers, and the difference between them is essential for how the organelle makes ATP.

Outer mitochondrial membrane
The outer membrane contains large channel-forming proteins called porins (also known as VDACs — voltage-dependent anion channels). These porins create wide pores that allow small molecules and ions — including ATP, ADP, pyruvate, and even small proteins — to pass freely between the cytoplasm and the intermembrane space (the region between the two membranes). Because of this, the intermembrane space has a similar small-molecule composition to the cytoplasm.

Inner mitochondrial membrane
The inner membrane is very different. It contains no porins and is almost completely impermeable — including to protons (H+). This tight seal is critical. During the electron transport chain, protons are actively pumped from the matrix (the interior of the mitochondrion) across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space. Because the inner membrane blocks their return, protons build up there, creating a steep electrochemical gradient.

The only efficient route for protons to flow back into the matrix is through ATP synthase, a protein complex embedded in the inner membrane. As protons flow through ATP synthase down their gradient, the energy released drives the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate. This coupling mechanism is called chemiosmosis.

The inner membrane is also extensively folded into structures called cristae, which dramatically increase its surface area. More surface area means more ATP synthase complexes can be packed in, boosting the cell's ATP output.

In summary: the outer membrane acts as a permeable outer fence, while the inner membrane is a tight energy-coupling barrier — and it is the impermeability of the inner membrane that makes ATP synthesis possible.
render.summary: The outer membrane is freely permeable to small molecules via porin channels. The inner membrane is tightly sealed, which traps protons in the intermembrane space and forces them through ATP synthase to generate ATP.
